summary: Pixel-identical to the original on the default rig at every realistic frame rate — same blue field, same 4-px red and 4-px green stripe pair, same 10 px/s scroll — differing only by a <=10/255 hue-constant rounding in the blue background and green stripe, plus a low-frame-rate scroll-tick quantisation the original has and the port does not.
observations: Single regime: a 300 s / 10 fps survey on both sides shows one unvarying look — solid blue field with one red 4-px stripe and one green 4-px stripe scrolling toward increasing pixel index. No modes, no palette walk, no drift; brightnessTrend 'steady' with meanBrightness min==max==88 (orig) / 85 (port) across 3000 frames.

Exact structure at 20 fps (--dump, 60 px strip, t=2 s): both sides draw background, then RED at indices 20-23, four background pixels, then GREEN at 28-31. Identical stripe widths (4 px each), identical 4-px gap, identical leading-edge index on both sides at every dumped time.

Motion: both scroll at exactly 10 px/s at fps 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 100 — green-stripe leading edge at 8,18,28,38,48 over t=0..4 s on both sides. Wrap period equals pixelCount/10 s (6 s on the 60 px default rig, 30 s on 300 px), confirmed identical on both sides.

Colour is the only default-rig difference. Original background is (0,10,255) and its green stripe is (5,255,0); the port uses (0,0,255) and (0,255,0). Red is (255,0,0) on both. That is hue 0.00/0.33/0.66 on the original vs 0/1/3, 2/3 exactly on the port — max channel delta 10/255 anywhere in any frame, visible in stats only as meanG 26 (orig) vs 17 (port).

Frame-rate coupling, on the ORIGINAL not the port: the original advances the stripe one whole pixel every ceil(fps/10) frames, so its speed is min(fps,10)/ceil(fps/10)*... measured as 3,4,5,6,8,10 px/s at fps 3,4,5,6,8,10; 6 px/s at 12 fps; ~7.7 px/s at 15 fps; 8 px/s at 16 and 24 fps; 10 px/s at 20,30,40,50,60,100 fps. The port holds a continuous 10 px/s at every rate tested. The two therefore coincide exactly at the harness default (20 fps) and at 10/30/40/50/60/100 fps, and differ by up to 25% at 12/15/16/24 fps.

The 5 fps survey is the artefact this creates: orig posted motion 11 and port 23 there, and the orig waterfall showed half as many stripe passes in 60 s. That is the original's tick quantisation at survey rate, not a port defect — at 20 fps the two waterfalls are indistinguishable.

Both sides are index-only, not (x,y)-driven, and identically so: on --rig grid --grid 32x8 both light only row 0 (flat indices 20-23 red, 28-31 green) with the remaining 7 rows solid background; on --pixels 300 both put the stripes at absolute indices 0-3 / 8-11 rather than scaling them to 5% of the strip; on --pixels 12 both wrap identically. Stripe width is a fixed 4 pixels regardless of rig size on both sides.
No randomness: seeds 1, 7 and 1234 render byte-identically on both sides. No clock dependence: --wall-clock 1756040000 reproduces the default run exactly on both sides.

Steady state confirmed: --skip 240 --seconds 12 at 20 fps has both sides on the same stripe indices at every dumped time (R0-3/G8-11 at t=240, 246; R20-23/G28-31 at 242, 248; R40-43/G48-51 at 244, 250). No decay, no freeze, no accumulation; zeroMotionFrames is 1 on both sides over 3000 frames.
Control surfaces match: --probe-controls reports '(no settable controls)' for BOTH sides, so the pattern genuinely has no dials and there is no control-surface asymmetry.
No compile or runtime errors on either side; wantsSensors false on both, so the sensor feed is a no-op here.
feedback: Colour constants: the original's non-red hues are 0.33 and 0.66, not 1/3 and 2/3. Using the exact thirds makes the port's background pure (0,0,255) and its green pure (0,255,0), where the original renders (0,10,255) and (5,255,0). Substituting the two-decimal hue values 0.33 and 0.66 would make the port byte-identical to the original on every frame tested. This is the ONLY difference at the default 20 fps rig — max 10/255 on one channel, invisible in practice.

Scroll timing: the original quantises the scroll to a whole-frame tick — it moves the stripe pair one integer pixel every ceil(fps/10) frames, targeting 10 px/s but landing on 6 px/s at 12 fps, ~7.7 at 15 fps and 8 at 16 and 24 fps. The port advances a continuous position at a true 10 px/s and is fps-invariant. They agree exactly at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 100 fps, so this only surfaces at odd intermediate frame rates. The port's behaviour is arguably the better one; flagging it only so a fixer knows the divergence exists and does not 'fix' the 5 fps survey mismatch by adding a wrong-direction change.

Nothing else to change: structure (4-px red stripe, 4-px gap, 4-px green stripe on a blue field), direction, wrap behaviour, rig-size scaling law (absolute pixel widths, not strip fractions), determinism, and the empty control surface all already match exactly.
